newsitem.title: USA: St. Petersburg riots expose deep racial divide.
newsitem.headline: St. Petersburg riots expose deep racial divide.

text.p: Gunfire and torchings have ended but fingerpointing and resentment were rampant on Friday after this city's second wave of racial unrest in a month reopened deep, unattended wounds.

The latest violence, sparked by a grand jury's refusal to charge a white police officer in the shooting of a black man, turned the spotlight on a little-known black militant group, the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement, which served notice that the black community's anger would not easily be soothed. "We will not live as a fearful community," Uhuru leader Omali Yeshitela said late on Thursday.

The southside St. Petersburg neighbourhood where the rioting took place was relatively calm overnight, authorities said, as police riding four and five to a squad car patroled streets ravaged 24 hours earlier by sniping and arson fires.
Officials said more than 100 fires earlier in the week caused at least $1 million in damage and a dozen people were wounded in the disturbance, the second in a month.

On Oct. 24, the city was convulsed by rioting after white St. Petersburg police officer James Knight shot and killed black motorist TyRon Lewis during a traffic stop. Wednesday's uprising followed a mostly grand jury's ruling that Knight's action was justifiable homicide.
"They didn't have to kill that man," Wilson Carter, 54, said as he stood near the charred shells of houses destroyed on Wednesday. "That's what it all boils down to."

In riots that ripped Miami in 1980, 1983 and 1989, black men were killed by white police officers who then, according to blacks, were treated leniently by the justice system. The worst urban riots this century, in Los Angeles in 1992, resulted from the acquittal of four policemen caught on videotape beating black motorist Rodney King.

As in those riots, the fatal shooting of Lewis was merely a spark that ignited the deep anger in the economically deprived black community, where residents say they are treated "like animals" by police and trodden by a judiciary too willing to permit white police to kill blacks in the streets.

"They look at you different if you are black," Rachel Hardy, 31, said as she stood before the smouldering ruins of a friend's home. "Everybody's not a drug dealer. Black people do have jobs. They work."

On Jackson Street, a knot of residents gathered in front of a home, their anger boiling over as they talked about Wednesday's outburst. They blamed police for the death of Lewis and the rioting that followed.

They said police had interfered with a meeting taking place at the Uhuru movement's headquarters two blocks away -- where a banner outside reads "We are our own liberators" -- and overreacted when a crowd failed to disperse as ordered.
"If they wouldn't have shot that tear gas none of this would have happened," one woman said.
